claim: SPARK is a transcriptional PPI reporter that improves upon yeast two-hybrid and TANGO designs by incorporating light-gating.
source: We previously reported 'SPARK', for 'Specific Protein Association tool giving transcriptional Readout with rapid Kinetics', a transcriptional PPI reporter that improves upon yeast two-hybrid and TANGO designs by incorporating light-gating.
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction and is supported by citation to the previous SPARK publication (Kim et al., 2017).

claim: Transcriptional activation in SPARK requires both a PPI event and the presence of blue light.
source: As shown in Figure 1A, transcriptional activation requires both a PPI event and the presence of blue light.
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1A showing the AND gate logic.

claim: Light-gating in SPARK dramatically reduces the background of the system.
source: Not only does the light-gating dramatically reduce the background of the system, but it also enables temporal specificity because the user can sync the light window to the biological time period of interest (e.g. just before or just after addition of a drug).
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction based on previous work with SPARK1.

claim: SPARK integrates PPI events over a 5 min user-selected time window determined by exogenous blue light delivery.
source: Instead of integrating PPI events over many hours or days, as yeast two-hybrid and TANGO do, SPARK integrates PPI events over just a 5 min user-selected time window determined by exogenous blue light delivery.
evidence: This is directly stated in the introduction as a feature of SPARK.

claim: SPARK1 performance is highly expression-level dependent due to its intermolecular design.
source: In working with first-generation SPARK (SPARK1), however, we noticed two limitations. The first is that, due to its intermolecular design, SPARK1 performance is highly expression-level dependent.
evidence: This is stated as an observed limitation in the introduction.

claim: When SPARK1 components are expressed at high levels, there is significant cleavage and TF release even when A-B interaction does not occur.
source: When SPARK1 components are expressed at high levels, however, TEVp interaction with TEVcs becomes proximity-independent, that is there is significant cleavage and TF release even when A-B interaction does not occur (likely because SPARK1 component levels exceed or are close to the TEVp-TEVcs Km which is estimated to be ~450 µM (Kapust et al., 2001; Kapust et al., 2002); Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated as an observation and supported by citation to TEVp-TEVcs Km values and illustrated in Figure 1C.

claim: The TEVp-TEVcs Km is estimated to be ~450 µM.
source: likely because SPARK1 component levels exceed or are close to the TEVp-TEVcs Km which is estimated to be ~450 µM (Kapust et al., 2001; Kapust et al., 2002)
evidence: This is stated with citation to published work.

claim: SPARK1 performance is best when the components are expressed stably or via viral transduction.
source: Our practical observation is that SPARK1 performance is best when the components are expressed stably or via viral transduction.
evidence: This is stated as a practical observation from working with SPARK1.

claim: Transient transfection methods such as lipofectamine or PEI result in higher expression levels and consequently high background for SPARK1.
source: Transient transfection methods such as lipofectamine or PEI result in higher expression levels and consequently high background.
evidence: This is stated as an observation about SPARK1 performance.

claim: Light delivery presents a technical challenge for high-throughput screens, particularly for robotic platforms.
source: The second limitation is that light delivery presents a technical challenge, particularly for high-throughput screens, as many robotic platforms are not equipped to dark-cage, deliver light, and then dark-cage again multiwell plates at specified timepoints.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of SPARK1 for high-throughput applications.

claim: SPARK2 incorporates a luciferase moiety to control the light-sensitive LOV domain.
source: Here, we report an improved, second-generation SPARK2 that incorporates a luciferase moiety to control the light-sensitive LOV domain.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as the key innovation of SPARK2.

claim: SPARK2 can be temporally gated by either external light or addition of a small-molecule luciferin.
source: SPARK2 can be temporally gated by either external light or addition of a small-molecule luciferin, which causes luciferase to open LOV via proximity-dependent BRET.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a key feature of SPARK2.

claim: Luciferase opens LOV via proximity-dependent BRET in SPARK2.
source: SPARK2 can be temporally gated by either external light or addition of a small-molecule luciferin, which causes luciferase to open LOV via proximity-dependent BRET.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated experimentally in the results.

claim: The nested 'AND' gate design of SPARK2 yields a lower-background system and improved PPI specificity.
source: Furthermore, the nested 'AND' gate design of SPARK2—in which both protease recruitment to the membrane-anchored transcription factor and LOV domain opening are regulated by the PPI of interest—yields a lower-background system and improved PPI specificity.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated in the results section.

claim: In SPARK2, both protease recruitment to the membrane-anchored transcription factor and LOV domain opening are regulated by the PPI of interest.
source: Furthermore, the nested 'AND' gate design of SPARK2—in which both protease recruitment to the membrane-anchored transcription factor and LOV domain opening are regulated by the PPI of interest—yields a lower-background system and improved PPI specificity.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract describing the nested AND gate design.

claim: SPARK2 was applied to high-throughput screening for GPCR agonists.
source: We apply SPARK2 to high-throughput screening for GPCR agonists and for the detection of trans-cellular contacts, all with versatile transcriptional readout.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated in Figure 4.

claim: SPARK2 was applied for the detection of trans-cellular contacts.
source: We apply SPARK2 to high-throughput screening for GPCR agonists and for the detection of trans-cellular contacts, all with versatile transcriptional readout.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated in Figure 5.

claim: NanoLuc is one of the brightest-emitting luciferase variants.
source: Among the ATP-independent variants, NanoLuc has been characterized as one of the brightest-emitting luciferase variants (England et al., 2016)
evidence: This is stated with citation to published characterization.

claim: NanoLuc's emission wavelength is 450 nm.
source: Among the ATP-independent variants, NanoLuc has been characterized as one of the brightest-emitting luciferase variants (England et al., 2016), and its emission wavelength (450 nm) overlaps with the activation spectrum of LOV.
evidence: This is stated directly in the text.

claim: NanoLuc's emission wavelength overlaps with the activation spectrum of LOV.
source: Among the ATP-independent variants, NanoLuc has been characterized as one of the brightest-emitting luciferase variants (England et al., 2016), and its emission wavelength (450 nm) overlaps with the activation spectrum of LOV.
evidence: This is stated directly in the text as a rationale for selecting NanoLuc.

claim: NanoLuc is 19 kDa in size.
source: NanoLuc's small size (19 kDa) also reduces potential steric problems when fused to other proteins
evidence: This is stated directly in the text.

claim: NanoLuc's substrate is furimazine.
source: and its substrate, furimazine, exhibits greater stability than the coelenterazine analogues used for RLuc, GLuc, and sbLuc (Hall et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated with citation to the NanoLuc characterization paper.

claim: Furimazine exhibits greater stability than the coelenterazine analogues used for RLuc, GLuc, and sbLuc.
source: and its substrate, furimazine, exhibits greater stability than the coelenterazine analogues used for RLuc, GLuc, and sbLuc (Hall et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated with citation to published work.

claim: In LOVTRAP, an engineered peptide Zdk1 binds to the C-terminus of the LOV domain in the dark.
source: In LOVTRAP, an engineered peptide Zdk1 binds to the C-terminus of the LOV domain in the dark.
evidence: This is stated as background on the LOVTRAP assay with citation.

claim: Upon blue light irradiation and LOV conformational change, the Zdk1 peptide diffuses away from the LOV domain in LOVTRAP.
source: Upon blue light irradiation and LOV conformational change, the Zdk1 peptide diffuses away from the LOV domain.
evidence: This is stated as background on the LOVTRAP assay with citation.

claim: The LOVTRAP system is reversible, such that termination of blue light results in Zdk1 rebinding to LOV.
source: The system is reversible, such that termination of blue light results in Zdk1 rebinding to LOV.
evidence: This is stated as background on the LOVTRAP assay with citation.

claim: Brief exposure to furimazine (10 µM for 1 min) caused mCherry-Zdk1 to rapidly relocalize from the membrane into the cytosol in the β2AR-NanoLuc-LOV LOVTRAP assay.
source: At baseline in the dark, we observed mCherry localization at the cell membrane, but in response to brief exposure to NanoLuc's substrate, furimazine (10 µM for 1 min), or to blue light (10 s), the mCherry rapidly relocalized into the cytosol (Figure 2B–C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2B-C.

claim: Brief exposure to blue light (10 s) caused mCherry-Zdk1 to rapidly relocalize from the membrane into the cytosol in the β2AR-NanoLuc-LOV LOVTRAP assay.
source: At baseline in the dark, we observed mCherry localization at the cell membrane, but in response to brief exposure to NanoLuc's substrate, furimazine (10 µM for 1 min), or to blue light (10 s), the mCherry rapidly relocalized into the cytosol (Figure 2B–C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2B-C.

claim: Comparable amounts of mCherry relocalization to cytosol were observed between furimazine and blue light conditions in the β2AR-NanoLuc-LOV LOVTRAP assay.
source: We observed comparable amounts of mCherry relocalization to cytosol between furimazine and blue light conditions (Figure 2D), suggesting that the NanoLuc-LOV activation was as efficient as exogenous blue light-LOV activation for releasing Zdk1.
evidence: This is stated in the text and quantified in Figure 2D.

claim: NanoLuc-LOV activation was as efficient as exogenous blue light-LOV activation for releasing Zdk1 in the LOVTRAP assay.
source: We observed comparable amounts of mCherry relocalization to cytosol between furimazine and blue light conditions (Figure 2D), suggesting that the NanoLuc-LOV activation was as efficient as exogenous blue light-LOV activation for releasing Zdk1.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the data in Figure 2D.

claim: The extracellular NanoLuc fusion construct (NanoLuc-β2AR-LOV) did not release mCherry-Zdk1 from the membrane in response to furimazine.
source: However, the extracellular fusion construct did not release mCherry-Zdk1 from the membrane in response to furimazine.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2F-H.

claim: Subsequent blue light delivered to cells with extracellular NanoLuc resulted in the release of mCherry-Zdk1, indicating the LOVTRAP construct was functional.
source: Subsequent blue light delivered to the same cell resulted in the release of mCherry-Zdk1, indicating the LOVTRAP construct was functional (Figure 2F–H).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2F-H.

claim: Robust NanoLuc bioluminescence emission was measured from both intracellular and extracellular NanoLuc fusion constructs.
source: To confirm that this difference was not due to higher expression levels of the intracellular NanoLuc versus extracellular NanoLuc fusions, we measured robust NanoLuc bioluminescence emission from both constructs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: NanoLuc activation of LOV is proximity-dependent.
source: From this experiment, we conclude that NanoLuc activation of LOV is proximity-dependent, as moving NanoLuc only ~5 nm away from LOV prevents its activation.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the extracellular vs intracellular NanoLuc experiments.

claim: Moving NanoLuc only ~5 nm away from LOV prevents its activation.
source: From this experiment, we conclude that NanoLuc activation of LOV is proximity-dependent, as moving NanoLuc only ~5 nm away from LOV prevents its activation.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the extracellular vs intracellular NanoLuc experiments.

claim: SPARK2 with NanoLuc-arrestin-TEVp gave clear light-dependent and isoetharine-dependent Citrine expression.
source: This 'SPARK2' tool gave clear light-dependent and isoetharine-dependent Citrine expression, as we previously observed with SPARK1, showing that introduction of 19 kD NanoLuc does not impair recognition or sterics (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: Introduction of 19 kD NanoLuc does not impair recognition or sterics in SPARK2.
source: This 'SPARK2' tool gave clear light-dependent and isoetharine-dependent Citrine expression, as we previously observed with SPARK1, showing that introduction of 19 kD NanoLuc does not impair recognition or sterics (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: Addition of isoetharine and 10 µM furimazine for 15 min results in robust Citrine expression ~8 hr later in SPARK2.
source: Figure 3B shows that addition of isoetharine and 10 µM furimazine for 15 min (rather than external blue light) results in robust Citrine expression ~8 hr later.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Minimal Citrine expression was observed in the absence of furimazine, or with furimazine but no isoetharine in SPARK2.
source: Minimal Citrine expression was observed in the absence of furimazine, or with furimazine but no isoetharine.
evidence: This is stated in the text referring to Figure 3B.

claim: SPARK2 reporters for AVPR2 and DRD1 both give furimazine- and agonist-dependent expression of Citrine.
source: Figure 3B shows that SPARK2 reporters for AVPR2 (arginine vasopressin receptor 2) and DRD1 (dopamine receptor type I) both give furimazine- and agonist-dependent expression of Citrine.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: NanoLuc can regulate the LOV domain of SPARK2 in place of external blue light.
source: Together, these results demonstrate that NanoLuc can indeed regulate the LOV domain of SPARK2 in place of external blue light, enabling users to toggle between luciferin-control and light-control of SPARK2 for PPI detection in living cells.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the SPARK2 experiments with multiple GPCRs.

claim: SPARK2 enables users to toggle between luciferin-control and light-control for PPI detection in living cells.
source: Together, these results demonstrate that NanoLuc can indeed regulate the LOV domain of SPARK2 in place of external blue light, enabling users to toggle between luciferin-control and light-control of SPARK2 for PPI detection in living cells.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the SPARK2 experiments.

claim: In SPARK1, TEVp recruitment to TEVcs depends on protein A-protein B interaction, but LOV-TEVcs uncaging depends only on exogenous blue light.
source: In SPARK1 (and in SPARK2 under light control), TEVp recruitment to TEVcs depends on protein A-protein B interaction, but LOV-TEVcs uncaging depends only on exogenous blue light.
evidence: This is stated as a description of SPARK1's mechanism.

claim: During the time period that LOV is open in SPARK1, even in the absence of an A-B interaction, TEVp may interact with TEVcs if expression levels approach the TEVp-TEVcs Km.
source: Thus, during the time period that LOV is open, even in the absence of an A-B interaction, TEVp may interact with TEVcs (if expression levels approach the TEVp-TEVcs Km).
evidence: This is stated as a rationale for the background observed in SPARK1.

claim: In luciferin-gated SPARK2, LOV-TEVcs uncaging is regulated by NanoLuc in a fashion that depends on A-B interaction.
source: This source of background should be eliminated when using luciferin-gated SPARK2, as LOV-TEVcs uncaging is regulated by NanoLuc in a fashion that depends on A-B interaction.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis for why SPARK2 should have lower background.

claim: When using luciferin-gated SPARK2, background Citrine signal was eliminated (no Citrine expression in the +luciferin/no PPI condition).
source: On the other hand, when we used luciferin (furimazine) to uncage the LOV domain instead of external blue light, we found that background Citrine signal was eliminated (no Citrine expression in the +luciferin/no PPI condition; Figure 3D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Substantial background was measured when light was delivered but isoetharine was omitted (+light/no PPI condition) in SPARK2.
source: The highest Citrine/HA intensity ratios were observed with external blue light and isoetharine (+light/PPI condition); however, we measured substantial background when light was delivered but isoetharine was omitted (+light/no PPI condition; Figure 3D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Robust Citrine/HA intensity ratios were observed when using luciferin and isoetharine (+luciferin/PPI condition) in SPARK2.
source: We could still observe robust Citrine/HA intensity ratios when using luciferin and isoetharine (+luciferin/PPI condition; Figure 3D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Luciferin-gating of SPARK2 produces higher PPI-specificity than light-gating.
source: We conclude that luciferin-gating of SPARK2 produces higher PPI-specificity than light-gating, due to the incorporation of a PPI-dependent BRET mechanism for LOV domain control that eliminates PPI-independent background.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the comparison experiments.

claim: SPARK2 with nested luciferase-gating produced a higher ±PPI signal ratio compared to SPARK1 with light-gating.
source: When directly compared to SPARK1 with light-gating, SPARK2 with nested luciferase-gating also produced a higher ±PPI signal ratio (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: The nested 'AND' gate via intramolecular BRET is essential for driving the improved specificity in PPI detection with SPARK2.
source: These data demonstrate that the nested 'AND' gate via intramolecular BRET is essential for driving the improved specificity in PPI detection with SPARK2.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the comparison of nested vs single AND gate designs.

claim: The single 'AND' gate design resulted in high background in the +furimazine/-PPI condition, comparable to the background observed with +light/-PPI.
source: Compared to the nested 'AND' gate design of SPARK2, the single 'AND' gate design resulted in high background in the +furimazine/-PPI condition, comparable to the background observed with +light/-PPI (Figure 3F–H).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3F-H.

claim: With 5 min of blue light, the NanoLuc-LOV fusion construct produced a similar ±PPI signal ratio as light-gating with SPARK2.
source: Importantly with 5 min of blue light, the NanoLuc-LOV fusion construct produced a similar ±PPI signal ratio as light-gating with SPARK2, suggesting that there is no steric hindrance due to the fusion of NanoLuc to LOV (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3H.

claim: There is no steric hindrance due to the fusion of NanoLuc to LOV.
source: Importantly with 5 min of blue light, the NanoLuc-LOV fusion construct produced a similar ±PPI signal ratio as light-gating with SPARK2, suggesting that there is no steric hindrance due to the fusion of NanoLuc to LOV (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the data in Figure 3H.

claim: FLuc uses an orthogonal substrate to NanoLuc (Beetle luciferin).
source: FLuc uses an orthogonal substrate to NanoLuc (Beetle luciferin) and also luminesces at a different wavelength (535 nm instead of 450 nm (Germain-Genevois et al., 2016); Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated with citation to published work.

claim: FLuc luminesces at 535 nm.
source: FLuc uses an orthogonal substrate to NanoLuc (Beetle luciferin) and also luminesces at a different wavelength (535 nm instead of 450 nm (Germain-Genevois et al., 2016); Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated with citation to published work.

claim: 11.6-fold higher FLuc luminescence was observed in cells exposed to furimazine and isoetharine for 20 min compared to cells exposed to only furimazine.
source: We observed 11.6-fold higher FLuc luminescence in cells exposed to furimazine and isoetharine for 20 min compared to cells exposed to only furimazine (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: There was no FLuc luminescence detected in the control conditions, confirming that only FLuc luminescence and not any cross-over NanoLuc luminescence was detected.
source: As there was no FLuc luminescence detected in the control conditions, this confirms that we are detecting only the FLuc luminescence and not any cross-over NanoLuc luminescence.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the FLuc reporter data.

claim: FLuc luminescence background is significant in the +light/no PPI condition but undetectable in the +furimazine/no PPI condition when SPARK2 is transiently expressed in HEK293T cells.
source: Figure 4B shows that when SPARK2 is transiently expressed in HEK293T cells, FLuc luminescence background is significant in the +light/no PPI condition but undetectable in the +furimazine/no PPI condition (both 5 min and 20 min treatments).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The highest ±PPI signal ratio is obtained with luciferin gating for 20 min in SPARK2.
source: The consequence is that the highest ±PPI signal ratio is obtained with luciferin gating for 20 min (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: At 5 min, the reduction in -PPI background with luciferin is offset by reduced +PPI signal, resulting in a lower ±PPI signal ratio compared to light-gating.
source: At 5 min, the reduction in -PPI background with luciferin is offset by reduced +PPI signal, resulting in a lower ±PPI signal ratio compared to light-gating.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the data in Figure 4B.

claim: Nested luciferin-gated SPARK2 is a lower-background, higher-specificity PPI reporter alternative to SPARK1/2 with light-gating.
source: Overall, these results, and the single cell imaging results above, support the notion that nested luciferin-gated SPARK2 is a lower-background, higher-specificity PPI reporter alternative to SPARK1/2 with light-gating.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the FLuc reporter experiments.

claim: For β2AR, several compounds with >3 fold increases in FLuc reporter expression relative to a DMSO vehicle control were detected, including known agonists such as isoproterenol, epinephrine, procaterol, cimaterol, and norepinephrine.
source: For β2AR, we detected several compounds with >3 fold increases in FLuc reporter expression relative to a DMSO vehicle control, including known agonists such as isoproterenol, epinephrine, procaterol, cimaterol, and norepinephrine (Figure 4E and Figure 4—source data 2).

claim: Weaker agonists such as the known partial β2AR agonist salbutamol and leflunomide drove 1.4- and 1.3-fold increases in FLuc reporter expression, respectively.
source: We could also detect weaker agonists such as the known partial β2AR agonist salbutamol and leflunomide, which drove 1.4- and 1.3-fold increases in FLuc reporter expression, respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the text referring to the drug screen results.

claim: Dopamine, which is a known β2AR partial agonist, did not drive an increase in FLuc expression in the β2AR SPARK2 screen.
source: Interestingly, dopamine, which is a known β2AR partial agonist, did not drive an increase in FLuc expression, supporting the notion that dopamine may act as a G-protein-biased β2AR partial agonist (Kobilka and Deupi, 2007; Swaminath et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citation to published work.

claim: Dopamine may act as a G-protein-biased β2AR partial agonist.
source: Interestingly, dopamine, which is a known β2AR partial agonist, did not drive an increase in FLuc expression, supporting the notion that dopamine may act as a G-protein-biased β2AR partial agonist (Kobilka and Deupi, 2007; Swaminath et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation with citation to published work.

claim: For DRD1, known partial and full agonists such as fenoldopam, cabergoline, apomorphine, and pergolide drove >6 fold increases in FLuc reporter expression.
source: For DRD1, we detected many more compounds that drove >1.5 fold increases in FLuc reporter expression. Notably, known partial and full agonists such as fenoldopam, cabergoline, apomorphine, and pergolide drove >6 fold increases in FLuc reporter expression (Figure 4E and Figure 4—source data 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Catecholamine β2AR agonists epinephrine and norepinephrine drove a 3- and 11-fold increase in FLuc expression for DRD1 activation.
source: Catecholamine β2AR agonists epinephrine and norepinephrine also drove a 3- and 11-fold increase in FLuc expression for DRD1 activation.
evidence: This is stated in the text referring to the DRD1 screen results.

claim: The anti-psychotic haloperidol, which is a known DRD2 antagonist, drove a two-fold increase in FLuc expression for DRD1 activation.
source: Surprisingly, the anti-psychotic haloperidol, which is a known DRD2 antagonist (Leysen et al., 1992), drove a two-fold increase in FLuc expression for DRD1 activation.
evidence: This is stated in the text with citation to published work.

claim: Haloperidol is a known DRD2 antagonist.
source: Surprisingly, the anti-psychotic haloperidol, which is a known DRD2 antagonist (Leysen et al., 1992), drove a two-fold increase in FLuc expression for DRD1 activation.
evidence: This is stated with citation to published work.

claim: β2AR-arrestin SPARK2 gives a 9.0-fold signal increase when agonist is added versus withheld (both in the presence of furimazine).

claim: The control condition with membrane-bound NanoLuc gave much lower reporter gene expression compared to β2AR-arrestin SPARK2.
source: Whereas β2AR-arrestin SPARK2 gives a 9.0-fold signal increase when agonist is added versus withheld (both in the presence of furimazine), the control condition gave much lower reporter gene expression (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Robust NanoLuc bioluminescence emission was measured from both NanoLuc-arrestin-TEVp and membrane-bound NanoLuc constructs.
source: Confirming that this difference was not due to higher expression levels of the NanoLuc-arrestin-TEVp compared to the membrane-bound NanoLuc, we measured robust NanoLuc bioluminescence emission from both constructs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).

claim: Comparable levels of FLuc reporter signal in response to agonist were measured for both NanoLuc-arrestin-TEVp and membrane-bound NanoLuc conditions when blue light was delivered instead of furimazine.

claim: NanoLuc must be in close proximity (<5 nm) to the LOV domain in order to efficiently mediate its opening.
source: These results again support the notion that NanoLuc must be in close proximity (<5 nm) to the LOV domain in order to efficiently mediate its opening.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the proximity-dependence experiments.

claim: oβ2AR is a chimera between bovine rhodopsin and β2AR.
source: For this system to work, oβ2AR (a chimera between bovine rhodopsin and β2AR (Airan et al., 2009)) must recruit NanoLuc-arrestin-TEVp upon activation, and NanoLuc must be able to activate oβ2AR in place of blue light.

claim: Gaussia luciferase has previously been fused to the N-terminus of channelrhodopsins to regulate their activity in vivo ('luminopsins').

claim: Luciferases have not previously been shown to turn on light-sensitive GPCR chimeras such as oβ2AR.
source: While Gaussia luciferase has previously been fused to the N-terminus of channelrhodopsins (Berglund et al., 2013; Berglund et al., 2016; Park et al., 2017) to regulate their activity in vivo ('luminopsins'), luciferases have not previously been shown to turn on light-sensitive GPCR chimeras such as oβ2AR.

claim: Significantly more Citrine-positive cells were observed in the +light/+9cr condition than in the +light/−9cr condition for oβ2AR SPARK2.

claim: Significantly more Citrine-positive cells were observed following 30 min of furimazine and 9cr compared to control conditions for oβ2AR SPARK2.

claim: Both extracellular NanoLuc-oβ2AR BRET and intracellular NanoLuc-LOV BRET are occurring in the same cells in the oβ2AR SPARK2 system.
source: These results suggest that both extracellular NanoLuc-oβ2AR BRET and intracellular NanoLuc-LOV BRET are occurring in the same cells, enabling TF release to produce reporter signal.

claim: 87% of all detected Citrine-positive Receiver cells were adjacent to an HA-positive Sender cell in the trans-cellular SPARK2 experiment.
source: To quantify specificity, we counted the fraction of Citrine-positive Receiver cells that were contacting HA-positive Sender cells (87%; n = 43 cells from 26 FOVs).
evidence: This is stated as a quantification of the trans-cellular SPARK2 specificity.

claim: A higher overall Citrine/Flag intensity ratio was observed in the condition with furimazine and Sender NanoLuc compared to control conditions with furimazine omitted or Sender NanoLuc omitted in trans-cellular SPARK2.
source: To quantify Citrine expression in all Receiver cells, we calculated the ratio of Citrine fluorescence to Flag immunostain detecting the oβ2AR component. We observed a higher overall Citrine/Flag intensity ratio in the condition with furimazine and Sender NanoLuc compared to control conditions with furimazine omitted or Sender NanoLuc omitted (Figure 5G and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5G.

claim: In the absence of 9cr, there was no significant increase in the Citrine/Flag intensity with either blue light or furimazine in trans-cellular SPARK2.
source: We confirmed that in the absence of 9cr, there was no significant increase in the Citrine/Flag intensity with either blue light or furimazine (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D–E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D-E.

claim: SPARK2 can be combined with intercellular NanoLuc-oβ2AR BRET to enable luciferin-gated, bioluminescence-mediated transcriptional readout of cell-cell contacts.
source: These results provide a proof-of-concept demonstration that SPARK2 can be combined with intercellular NanoLuc-oβ2AR BRET to enable luciferin-gated, bioluminescence-mediated transcriptional readout of cell-cell contacts.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the trans-cellular SPARK2 experiments.

claim: SPARK2 employs a novel design not previously used for PPI detection.
source: SPARK2 employs a novel design not previously used for PPI detection.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion.

claim: Via a single modification of SPARK1—addition of a luciferase moiety onto the protease component of SPARK—SPARK2 gains two new capabilities: the ability to toggle between light-gating and luciferin-gating for temporal specificity, and greatly reduced background leading to a more PPI-specific tool.
source: Via a single modification of SPARK1—addition of a luciferase moiety onto the protease component of SPARK—SPARK2 gains two new capabilities: the ability to toggle between light-gating and luciferin-gating for temporal specificity, and greatly reduced background leading to a more PPI-specific tool.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of SPARK2's improvements.

claim: SPARK2 could be used to detect transient arrestin recruitment to several activated GPCRs, giving stable and versatile (Citrine, FLuc) reporter gene readout many hours later.
source: We showed that SPARK2 could be used to detect transient arrestin recruitment to several activated GPCRs, giving stable and versatile (Citrine, FLuc) reporter gene readout many hours later.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of SPARK2 applications.

claim: Using luciferin-gating, SPARK2 was used for high-throughput compound screening against activation of two GPCRs.
source: Using luciferin-gating, we used SPARK2 for high-throughput compound screening against activation of two GPCRs.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of SPARK2 applications.

claim: The SPARK2 design was extended to detection of cell-cell contacts, employing trans-cellular luciferase activation of a GPCR-rhodopsin chimera.
source: We also extended the SPARK2 design to detection of cell-cell contacts, employing trans-cellular luciferase activation of a GPCR-rhodopsin chimera.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of SPARK2 applications.

claim: At the heart of SPARK2 is a proximity-dependent interaction between the blue light-emitting luciferase NanoLuc and the blue-light absorbing photosensory domain LOV.
source: At the heart of SPARK2 is a proximity-dependent interaction between the blue light-emitting luciferase NanoLuc and the blue-light absorbing photosensory domain LOV.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of the SPARK2 mechanism.

claim: Luciferase can regulate the activity of LOV domains.
source: Here, we continue the trend by showing that luciferase can also regulate the activity of LOV domains.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a novel finding.

claim: Luciferase regulation of LOV is proximity-dependent, both in the context of LOVTRAP and SPARK2.
source: We further demonstrate that such regulation is proximity-dependent, both in the context of LOVTRAP and SPARK2.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a key finding.

claim: If LOV-based optogenetic tools were to incorporate NanoLuc, this would enable users to toggle between light control and luciferin control.
source: It seems likely that if these tools were to also incorporate NanoLuc, this would enable users to toggle between light control and luciferin control, as we do for SPARK2.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation about future applications.

claim: One could envision tool variants in which LOV-mediated functions are conditional upon PPIs or subcellular localization events designed by the user.
source: Furthermore, because we have shown that luciferase-LOV regulation is proximity-dependent, one could envision tool variants in which LOV-mediated functions (PPI induction, protein inactivation/activation, channel opening, etc.) are conditional upon PPIs or subcellular localization events designed by the user.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation about future applications.

claim: Luciferase regulation is likely to extend beyond LOVs.
source: Finally, we note that luciferase regulation is likely to extend beyond LOVs.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation based on the findings.

claim: Cryptochromes (e.g. CRY-CIBN) also contain blue-light excitable flavin cofactors.
source: Cryptochromes (e.g. CRY-CIBN (Kennedy et al., 2010)) also contain blue-light excitable flavin cofactors
evidence: This is stated with citation to published work.

claim: Luciferase can regulate oβ2AR, a retinal-containing blue-light activated GPCR-rhodopsin chimera.
source: and we showed here that luciferase can also regulate oβ2AR, a retinal-containing blue-light activated GPCR-rhodopsin chimera.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a finding from the trans-cellular experiments.

claim: A 'double filter' or nested 'AND' gate concept could be incorporated into a range of other reporter designs, particularly those with limited dynamic range.
source: We envision that the 'double filter' or nested 'AND' gate concept could also be incorporated into a range of other reporter designs, particularly those with limited dynamic range.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation about future applications.

claim: There are numerous examples of natural pathways that incorporate 'double filters' to increase specificity, such as tRNA synthetases that catalyze amino acid loading onto cognate tRNAs.
source: Interestingly, there are numerous examples of natural pathways that incorporate 'double filters' to increase specificity, such as tRNA synthetases that catalyze amino acid loading onto cognate tRNAs (Fersht and Dingwall, 1979).
evidence: This is stated with citation to published work.

claim: Trans-cellular SPARK2 has complementary features to existing methods for probing cell-cell contacts, although further optimization and characterization are required to make it a broadly useful tool.
source: Trans-cellular SPARK2 has complementary features to these existing methods, although further optimization and characterization are required to make it a broadly useful tool for the study of trans-cellular interactions.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an assessment of trans-cellular SPARK2.

claim: The LOV domain contains a flavin chromophore that covalently reacts with cysteine 450 upon irradiation with 450 nm blue light.
source: The LOV domain contains a flavin chromophore that covalently reacts with cysteine 450 upon irradiation with 450 nm blue light.
evidence: This is stated as background on LOV domain mechanism.

claim: Blue light irradiation drives a large conformational change of LOV's C-terminal J-alpha helix.
source: This in turn drives a large conformational change of LOV's C-terminal J-alpha helix (Harper et al., 2003), which can expose or conceal recognition sites, such as TEVcs.
evidence: This is stated with citation to published work.

claim: Cell death can be mediated by the action of luciferase on the flavin-containing protein miniSOG.
source: A recent report describes that cell death can be mediated by the action of luciferase on the flavin-containing protein miniSOG (Proshkina et al., 2018), suggesting that luciferase-catalyzed uncaging of asLOV2 may also be possible.
evidence: This is stated with citation to published work.

claim: VLuc requires ATP to produce bioluminescence, limiting it to intracellular use.
source: Whereas VLuc requires ATP to produce bioluminescence, limiting it to intracellular use, the others do not (Tung et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with citation to published work.

claim: The asLOV2 V416L mutation slows its off kinetics (return to the dark state conformation).
source: The asLOV2 contains a V416L mutation that slows its off kinetics (return to the dark state conformation), and consequently slows the rate of Zdk1 recapture (V416L reset t1/2=496 s).
